Nvidia ( NVDA , +0.8%) bounced late and finished in the middle of the pack among Dow Jones stocks , as receding AI fear ultimately overcame company-specific loathing.

Indeed, the VanEck Semiconductor ETF ( SMH ) was up 4.2% today, as other chipmakers caught plenty of bids. And Anthropic ( ANT ) surged 11% in further affirmation of renewed faith in the broader AI trade.

Colin Montgomery suggests that expectations should be properly managed. Plus letters from Paul Hartley, Hartley Dean and Peter Thornton

John Harris’s jeremiad about what the world of work has become (A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue, 22 November) put me in mind of the old joke: “How do I get to Dublin?” “Well, I wouldn’t start from here.” Because, as he concludes, there’s almost no chance of any government being able to even begin to relieve this situation quickly, short of putting an emergency brake on 40 years of neoliberalism. As if.

I’d like to suggest a real starting point for the fightback against this seemingly interminable malaise that looks set to blight generations to come: namely, begin from somewhere grounded in properly managed expectations. Because arguably, that’s what underpins all of this: we’ve all been cynically inveigled into a bargain that can never be fulfilled.

items.title: The Best Stocks of the Past 8 Decades
items.summary:
Kiplinger Personal Finance Magazine is celebrating its 80th birthday . In honor of that, we're sharing articles from the 80th-anniversary print edition, including this look back in history. 

In the very first issue of Kiplinger Magazine , published in January 1947, the editors forecast rocky times economically but said they wouldn't last long. "People need and want millions of homes, automobiles, refrigerators, electrical appliances, tables and beds and chairs, and dozens of new and better services."

Well, that just about nailed the next 80 years. The story of the post-WWII American economy has been rising standards of living for the consumer, handsome profits for corporate America and growing fortunes for the people who have bankrolled much of the progress by investing in the stock market.

Certainly, the climb hasn't been consistently upward. We've had a dozen bear markets (drops of 20% or more), including meltdowns in 1987 and 2001 and the housing-driven debacle of 2007–09 that ushered in a financial crisis that led to the Great Recession. We've also had some fabulous bull runs, including at least three tech-fueled booms. We watched the Nifty Fifty and the Magnificent Seven soar, saw the cost of trading plummet, and witnessed the rise of do-it-yourself investors who have taken the reins of their own financial security.

Overall, the U.S. stock market has been a supreme engine of wealth creation, dependable if sometimes rocky. And the stocks that dominated help tell the story. As we celebrate Kiplinger Personal Finance 's 80th anniversary , we decided to look back at…
items.t: The Best Stocks of the Past 8 Decades

items.title: How to Update Your Estate Plan for Every Stage of Life
items.summary:
Estate planning at any age requires individuals and couples to make countless important decisions. 

From choosing executors and guardians to selecting life insurance and creating health proxies, everyone must make dozens of consequential decisions simply to begin the process.

After drafting their initial estate plans, individuals and couples may believe that they can close the book on this chapter in their lives. That's a mistake. Estate planning is not a set- it-and-forget-it proposition. 

As individuals, couples and families grow and age, they should regularly review and update their estate plans to ensure that they're current and in keeping with their life circumstances.

Here are some helpful tips for individuals, couples and families to guide their estate planning activities at all stages of their lives:

Young couples When couples have their first child, they usually think about estate planning. At the outset, they'll have three important decisions to make:

Who will be their child's guardian and care for them physically? Who will distribute assets contained in a will? The couple may need to designate a trustee, who oversees a trust and makes financial decisions on behalf of beneficiaries The couple can choose the same individual to serve in all three roles or designate different people for each. The key is to choose people based on their ability to fulfill each role and responsibility, not simply due to family relationships or proximity.

items.title: Use Trump Accounts to Teach Your Kids Investing
items.summary:
I was looking forward to writing a column about investing with kids because for the first time, one of my grandchildren, 9-year-old Bolton, expressed an interest in investing. But when I sat down to interview Bolton, the story got even better. I asked him what had inspired him, and he said, "It was a book you bought me, Grammy."

I was floored. The book was 50 Math Tricks That Will Change Your Life , by Tanya Zakowich, and what specifically caught his eye was the rule of 72 : Divide 72 by the rate of return on your investment and you'll know how long it will take to double your money. That bit of info sent Bolton to the stocks app on his dad's phone to check the rate of return on various stocks, and after that, he was off and running. 

He got a helping hand from his dad, my older son, John, who had already opened an account with Greenlight , an online money management system that lets families track their kids' saving and spending. Greenlight charges a monthly fee of $5.99 that covers up to five children, and for an extra $5, you can enroll in an investing option that lets kids buy fractional shares.

Bolton initially invested $50 in Intel and $40 in PayPal; he later sold PayPal for a $16 profit and is still hanging on to Intel. He and his dad have also watched a number of instructional videos, and "they can even recommend an exchange-traded fund based on your investing interests ," says Bolton.

John notes that the fees are higher than you would pay with a traditional brokerage account. [Note: Fidelity account holders can open a no-fee Youth Account for teens ages 13 to…

items.title: Ask the Editor: Questions on the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax
items.summary:
Each week in our Ask the Tax Editor series, Joy Taylor, The Kiplinger Tax Letter editor, answers questions on topics submitted by readers. This week, she's looking at four tax questions from readers on the 3.8% tax on net investment income, or NII. ( Get a free issue of The Kiplinger Tax Letter or subscribe .) 

1. What is the NII tax? Question: I read a recent story in Kiplinger Personal Finance magazine that referred to a net investment income (NII) tax. I have never heard about this tax. Can you explain it? 

Joy Taylor: The 3.8% net investment income tax, which was enacted as part of Obamacare , applies to single filers with modified adjusted gross income (AGI) above $200,000 and to joint filers with modified AGIs over $250,000. The income threshold is $125,000 for married people filing separately. 

Trusts and estates can also be hit with the surtax if their 2026 AGI exceeds $16,000 and they have undistributed net investment income. 

Here, modified AGI is AGI plus tax-free foreign-earned income. The tax is due on the smaller of net investment income (NII) or the excess of modified AGI over the set income thresholds.

NII includes dividends, capital gains , taxable interest, annuities , royalties, passive rents and certain income from passive activities. Trade or business income derived through a passive activity is also NII, provided that the business income isn’t otherwise subject to self-employment tax. Distributions from 401(k)s , IRAs , pensions, and the like are not investment income. Nor is tax-exempt interest from municipal bonds.

items.title: 4 Ways for Couples to Stop Fighting About Finances
items.summary:
Money can be one of the most difficult subjects to discuss with people closest to us. Whether you're discussing spending habits with a spouse or making plans for the future with a new partner, differences in financial priorities can quickly become a source of tension. 

But as living costs, credit card debt and concerns about job security continue to rise, these conversations are increasingly important for households trying to balance immediate needs with long-term financial goals.

The challenge is that our attitudes toward money are shaped by much more than our current financial circumstances. Childhood experiences , family dynamics and personal values all influence how we save, spend and make financial decisions. 

Understanding those influences, both in ourselves and in others, can make it easier to approach difficult conversations with empathy rather than judgment. Here are four ways to navigate financial disagreements and work toward common goals.

1. Understand where the other person is coming from Everyone brings their own financial history into a relationship. Someone who grew up in a household where money was tight may approach spending very differently from someone who rarely had to worry about whether their family could afford something. 

These early experiences often shape our financial habits well into adulthood, even when our circumstances have changed.

items.title: Cut Financial Advice Fees by Paying Only for Planning
items.summary:
A 1% advisory fee on a $2 million portfolio is $20,000 a year. If the help you really need is a retirement plan or an answer to one specific financial question, it's worth asking whether you could buy that advice separately and spend less. 

The answer will depend on the services you use, the price of a planner and how much investment work you can handle yourself.

The funny Liberty Mutual commercials with Doug in his yellow shirt and his feathered co-worker, LiMu Emu, offer a memorable rule: "Only pay for what you need." 

Apply that idea to financial advice. If you want to know whether you can afford to retire , buy a home or change jobs, you might be able to hire a qualified financial planner for that work without paying someone to manage your investment accounts year after year.

"Know what you're getting and what you're paying," Steven Fox , CFP®, EA told me when I interviewed him for my second book, tentatively titled FeeSmart for the Individual Investor: How Savvy Investors Avoid Overpaying for Financial Advice .

In the book, I'm developing strategies to help individual investors calculate what they currently pay for financial advice and find opportunities to significantly reduce advisory fees when the services they need can be obtained for less. 

Fox, a CFP® professional and enrolled agent, founded AdviceOnly , a firm that supports planners who provide financial planning without managing client investments or selling financial products. His advice is a useful starting point for anyone reviewing an existing financial advisory relationship or shopping for one.

items.title: 7 Ways to Save Money on Heating Oil This Winter

With colder temperatures approaching, households in colder regions are bracing for higher heating costs, especially those that rely on heating oil. 

Unlike households that rely on natural gas or electricity, homeowners who use heating oil often must purchase fuel in large quantities, sometimes spending hundreds of dollars on a single delivery. When prices rise, those costs can add up quickly.

According to the National Energy Assistance Directors Association (NEADA), households that rely on heating oil could see their seasonal heating bills jump by as much as 70%, reaching approximately $2,977. That's a significant increase for families already juggling higher costs for groceries, housing and other essentials.

While there's no way to know exactly how much you'll spend on heating this season, you still have some control of the expense. From shopping around for suppliers to making a few energy-efficient upgrades, here are seven ways to keep your home comfortable without overpaying this winter.

Start by requesting quotes from at least three local suppliers and comparing their prices per gallon. Ask about minimum delivery requirements, additional fees and whether the quoted price applies to one-time purchases or requires enrollment in an automatic delivery program.

This Thanksgiving, consider taking stock of what you already have — and how a little gratitude can help you make the most of it.

items.title: How to Give Your Grandkids Your Attention This Thanksgiving
items.summary:
Ron and Marilyn spent two days preparing for Thanksgiving last year. Marilyn made her mother's cornbread stuffing and three kinds of pie. Ron pulled the table leaf from storage so all 11 of them could sit at one table.

The family arrived a little after noon. Within an hour, Ron noticed his 15-year-old granddaughter, Abi, scrolling on her phone under the table. "Can you put that down for one day?" he said, loud enough for everyone to hear. "Your grandmother and I won't be around forever."

Abi put the phone away. She also said very little for the rest of the afternoon. By 4 o'clock, coats were coming off the hooks.

That night, Marilyn said what both of them were feeling: "We did everything for them, and they couldn't wait to leave."

Ron and Marilyn are generous, loving people. They also made a mistake that is common among grandparents, and it is easy to miss because it looks like love. They expected to receive attention during Thanksgiving instead of giving it. Their family could feel it.

Gratitude flows outward Thanksgiving is the one holiday built around gratitude , and most of us think of gratitude as something we feel. It is better understood as something we do, and it has a direction.

Psychologist Sara Algoe's research on what she calls the "find, remind and bind" function of gratitude offers a useful lens. Gratitude helps us find the people worth investing in, reminds us of the relationships we already have and binds us more closely to them.

items.title: I tried leaving all my money to my sister. She said no – and forced me to think about who really needs it
items.summary:
I thought making a will would be easy. Somehow, I ended up grilling my friends about their finances

I’ve spent a lot of my life thinking about death. When I was six, my dad had a heart attack. He had been our primary caregiver – the person who took us to school, took us to play in the park and bought us takeaways (the sweet man’s skills didn’t extend to the kitchen). The day it happened, my sister and I were rushed to A&E so we could see him lying wordless in a bay in case he didn’t live. Though he did survive, he never recovered and the threat of death hung over the household. It delivered on its promise when I was 18.

Rather than feeling relief that his suffering was over and the purgatory of sickness was done, I turned to worrying incessantly about the health of my mother. Because my parents were immigrants, they had no family in Britain – no one they could ask to watch us for a couple of hours without payment, let alone look out for us after they were gone. So, just before I started secondary school, my mum asked one of my friends’ parents if she could name them as our next of kin. They said yes, but not wanting to rely on others, she continued to work hard to ensure we, as well as her family in Iraq, would have as much financial security as possible.

Indeed, all three indexes finished well above their intraday lows heading into Thursday's Thanksgiving break, with Papa Dow and the Nasdaq coming back from 1,000-point-plus pre-lunch declines.

items.title: 10 Things You Should Know About the Inheritance Talk
items.summary:
More than $120 trillion will pass between generations over the next two decades. Members of the baby boomer and Silent generations managed to accumulate unprecedented amounts of wealth as the stock market became more accessible, homeownership and home values rose, and retirement tools like 401(k)s and IRAs turned workers into long-term savers and investors. 

But as bank accounts and net worths swelled, Americans didn't all suddenly become comfortable talking about money. 

Kiplinger commissioned Morning Consult to conduct a survey to better understand Americans' feelings and beliefs about inheritance , including how prepared they feel – and how prepared they actually are. The survey reached 2,500 adult children (ages 25-60) with at least one living parent and 2,500 people aged 55+ with at least one adult child. Our research uncovered many potential problems in families' futures, many of which could be solved with open, ongoing conversation. 

Here are 10 things we learned:

1. More parents plan to leave an inheritance than children expect one Our research showed there's already a disconnect at a very basic level of understanding. Nearly 50% of the parent generation said they plan to leave a meaningful inheritance, but only 24% of children are expecting one. 

Additionally, there's a disconnect in expectations of what makes up parents' estates. Half of parents said traditional or Roth IRAs and 401(k)s are in their estate, but only a third of the younger generation said they believe that's in their parents' estate. Moreover, 54% of parents said real estate is in their…
items.t: 10 Things You Should Know About the Inheritance Talk

items.title: How to Cure Financial FOMO With the 48-Hour Rule
items.summary:
It's easier than ever to start comparing our lives to thousands of others at the touch of a button. 

Log in to any social media platform of your choice and you're bound to see someone post about buying a home or car, getting married, taking a dream vacation or even retiring . Or, a company or influencer will be trying to sell you a product or service. 

All of that exposure can make it feel like you have to make the purchase or do the thing to keep up, but over time, those feelings can come at a financial cost.

If you've felt financial FOMO , the financial fear of missing out, you're far from alone. Four in five Americans say the financial situations of people close to them have influenced how they view their own finances, according to a 2026 survey from the CFP Board . 

Last year, 51% of U.S. adults made an investment or purchase because of financial FOMO, according to a survey from Empower .

Although these feelings are common, spending more than you can afford to avoid the fear of missing out can quickly become a problem. 

I know because I did it.

items.title: Tax-Smart Strategies for Charitable Giving
items.summary:
Most of us give from the heart. And as icing on the cake, getting a tax deduction for your charitable contributions is a nice reward for your generosity. In recent years, however, those who claimed the standard deduction on their tax return — the majority of taxpayers — had to be satisfied with a thank-you note from the charities they supported, because only taxpayers who itemized could deduct their contributions. 

That will change, starting this year. A provision in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act will allow taxpayers who claim the standard deduction to deduct some of their charitable contributions. Another provision could encourage more taxpayers to itemize, enabling them to deduct even more of their contributions. 

But the OBBBA contains some downsides for givers, too. The law places a new limit on the amount itemizers can deduct, and it imposes additional restrictions on philanthropists who are in the top tax bracket. 

That doesn’t mean you should cut back on your giving. You’ll just need to be more strategic to get the most value for your charitable contributions. Look at it this way: Lowering your tax bill as much as possible now will give you that much more money to donate next year. 

And there’s no shortage of worthwhile organizations that need help.

Make the most of new rules. Starting with the 2026 tax year, taxpayers who claim the standard deduction can deduct up to $1,000 in cash donations to charities, or up to $2,000 for married couples who file jointly. 

This is significant because since the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act nearly doubled the standard…

items.title: How to Realistically Manage an Exit From Your Business
items.summary:
Most business owners I meet have a number in mind. It's what they believe their company could sell for someday: $5 million, $10 million, perhaps considerably more.

While they know this number, they often haven't calculated what they need from the business to fund the next stage of their lives. That's usually a very different sum.

An owner may believe selling your business for $6 million means having $6 million in cash available for retirement. But taxes, debt, transaction expenses, deal structure and other factors can significantly reduce what ultimately becomes investable wealth.

And that's only part of the equation.

For many entrepreneurs, the company is not simply an asset. It may pay their salary, provide distributions, cover health insurance, vehicles and travel, and fund other expenses that will eventually move from the company balance sheet to their personal one.

That's why I believe business owners should approach an exit from two directions at once: 

What is the business likely to be worth, and what does my life require it to be worth?

I have spent most of my time since the turn of the 21st century thinking about the process of investing. This includes topics such as market efficiency (where and how price and value diverge), valuation, competitive strategy analysis, and decision-making.

(Image credit: Harriman House / Pan Macmillan) We know substantially more about each of these areas today than we did in 1986, but there remains a vast amount to learn. items.title: Is Your Financial Adviser Using AI and Your Data Safely?
items.summary:
Producing a polished explanation of a complex financial topic has become easier. Artificial intelligence (AI) can summarize research, organize information and draft an email in seconds. But deciding whether that explanation is accurate and useful still takes human work.

For a financial practice, it could be tempting to measure progress by how much faster things get done. Investors generally have a more practical interest: That the service helps them understand their choices and make informed decisions.

In my work with financial professionals, I view technology through the lens of the person receiving the service. If an AI tool helps a practice work faster, what improves for you? Better preparation, clearer explanations and more thoughtful follow-through are useful places to start.

Used responsibly, it can strengthen the preparation and communication behind a financial relationship. Its usefulness depends on someone knowing what to do with the output, including when to question it .

Put better preparation to work Some of the most practical applications are straightforward. FINRA's 2026 regulatory oversight report points out that summarizing documents and extracting information are the leading generative AI use cases among its member firms. Drafting content and automating workflows are other documented uses.

Within approved procedures, a financial professional could use AI to organize public research, develop a general meeting agenda or prepare an initial explanation of a financial concept. Each still needs review before it informs a discussion or reaches you.

items.title: Can the Fed Tackle Stubborn Inflation?
items.summary:
To help you understand what is going on in the economy our highly experienced Kiplinger Letter team will keep you abreast of the latest developments and forecasts ( Get a free issue of The Kiplinger Letter or subscribe ). You'll get all the latest news first by subscribing, but we will publish many (but not all) of the forecasts a few days afterward online. Here’s the latest… 

Inflation is too high. You know it. We know it. The question: When will it get under control? And what will it take to achieve that? After five years of inflation exceeding the Federal Reserve’s goal of 2%, what must the Fed do to rein it in, and at what cost? 

Inflation, now near 4%, can get down to 3%, we think. The gradually higher interest rates the Fed is preparing to implement should help a bit. So will the calendar, as the year-over-year comparison the government uses to calculate inflation each month stops being worsened by this year’s energy price spike. Fuel prices will still be high next spring, but not higher than they were 12 months earlier. That effect alone will yield some good monthly inflation reports. 2027 may even sport a benign headline inflation rate. 

But... Inflation outside of energy is too entrenched after years of running high. This began amid COVID-19 and continued afterward, when wage gains shot up. Now, you see the resulting price rises in many services: Medical care, car repairs, water service, trash pickup, yard work, entertainment, etc. a relentless incline. 

Goods prices aren’t helping. Normally, goods tend to decline a bit in price over time as manufacturers find…
items.t: Can the Fed Tackle Stubborn Inflation?
